analysis.one_liner: Makes it harder and slower for regulators to label big insurers and asset managers as systemically risky.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill 44-12 with 60 bipartisan cosponsors, but the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites how the Financial Stability Oversight Council (FSOC) decides which large nonbank financial companies — big insurers, asset managers, and similar firms — must submit to Federal Reserve oversight and stricter "prudential" rules. It would require regulators to first consider lighter-touch alternatives, give companies written notice, hearings, and the right to submit plans to fix their own risks, and let companies request reevaluation of their designation every five years. It also adds transparency requirements, including a public explanation of the basis for each designation. The House Financial Services Committee approved it with a large bipartisan vote, but it never reached the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Large nonbank financial companies — life insurers, asset managers, and other big firms facing or fearing FSOC designation as systemically important. They would gain advance notice, hearings, the right to contest designations and propose their own mitigation plans, a requirement that regulators try other options first, annual reevaluation of existing designations, and a five-year window to request reevaluation. The public also gets something: FSOC would have to publicly explain the basis for each final designation and publish the metrics it uses to pick companies for review.

how_it_helps.text: Requires FSOC to weigh whether imposing Federal Reserve prudential standards is appropriate versus other, lighter forms of regulation before designating a nonbank company.
Gives nonbank companies written notice, at least 30 days to submit materials contesting a determination, and a chance to meet with the Council — plus an annual reevaluation of every designation.

Lets a company request reevaluation of its designation every five years, appear with counsel, submit a plan to modify its business, and get extensions on implementation timelines approved by the Council.

Raises the voting bar: FSOC needs a two-thirds vote including the Chair to propose or make a determination, and must give the company's primary regulator at least 180 days to address identified risks with its own rules before FSOC can act.

Adds public transparency: FSOC must publicly explain the basis for final designations, report annually on how many companies it is reviewing, and publish the thresholds and metrics used to identify companies for analysis.

analysis.who_pays: If a large nonbank firm's risks are addressed only through slower, weaker measures — or a designation is delayed or avoided through the new hearing-and-plan process — the cost falls on the financial system and, through bailout risk in a crisis, on taxpayers and ordinary depositors and policyholders. Consumers can also pay through less vigorous oversight of firms whose failure could ripple through the economy.

drawbacks.text: The bill layers months of process onto each designation: a primary regulator gets at least 180 days to respond, companies get 30-day windows to submit materials, hearings, and plan revisions — time during which an identified risk can keep growing.

FSOC cannot propose a designation until it first finds the company's primary regulator's own actions insufficient to mitigate the risks, which pushes oversight toward the lighter-touch regulators the company already answers to.

Annual reevaluation plus company-submitted mitigation plans with discretionary extensions give designated firms recurring opportunities to negotiate their way out of, or defer, stricter Federal Reserve supervision.
Requiring a two-thirds vote including the Chair for every step makes it easier for any determined holdouts on the Council to block a designation altogether.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill has a real upside — more due process for targeted companies and genuinely useful public transparency about how FSOC picks and designates firms. But its main effect runs the other way: it makes each designation slower, more contested, and easier to avoid or unwind, moving oversight of the largest nonbank firms toward less demanding regulators. An honest supporter has to acknowledge that the price of the added process is a bigger chance that a systemic risk goes unaddressed until it becomes a crisis, when the fallout lands on taxpayers and the public rather than the firm.

outcome.mechanism: The House Financial Services Committee approved it, but the bill sat on the House calendar and never came up for a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dennis Ross introduced the bill on March 23, 2015, with Rep. John Delaney as an original cosponsor, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The committee held markup sessions on November 3-4, 2015, and ordered the bill reported by a vote of 44 to 12.
The bill attracted 60 cosponsors — 31 Democrats and 29 Republicans.
The committee reported the bill without amendment on December 12, 2016 (H. Rept. 114-871), and it was placed on the Union Calendar, House Calendar No. 681.
The House never took up the bill, and it died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public and financial regulators came out no worse off: the existing, stricter FSOC designation process stayed in place, and the large nonbank financial firms that backed the bill gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regulators and the public; big nonbank firms gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: The bill was genuinely bipartisan: 31 of 188 House Democrats and 29 of 247 House Republicans cosponsored it, and the committee approved it 44-12.

industries.industry: Large nonbank financial companies (life insurers, asset managers)
industries.note: The bill would hand these firms — the ones FSOC designates as systemically important — advance notice, hearings, appeal rights, self-authored mitigation plans, and annual and five-year reevaluation chances, making designation and continued Fed supervision harder to obtain and keep. Their gain is lighter oversight of firms whose failure could force public backstops, so their interest runs against stronger crisis prevention for ordinary people.

The bill would constrain regulators' ability to designate and supervise systemically risky nonbank firms, requiring two-thirds votes, 180-day handoffs to primary regulators, and consideration of lighter alternatives. Regulators' interest in keeping that authority runs alongside the public's interest in crisis prevention.
